  <entry>
    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34803v1</id>
    <title>An event is a set, not a number: building the algebra of events before the probability measure in a school progression</title>
    <updated>2026-10-26T03:42:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34803v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.34803v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Asked what an event is, pupils often answer with a fraction. This paper argues that school probability should separate two learnings and order them: the algebra of events (random experiment, outcomes, sample space, events as sets of outcomes, the operations not, or, and) and the probability measure, which attaches a number to each event. Before learning to compute the probability of an event, pupils should learn to build, identify and handle the event. The thesis rests on the structure of finite probability, in which the rules are facts about events carried over by an additive function, and on the history of the subject, in which errors such as d'Alembert's two tosses concerned the weighting of outcomes and were resolved by refining events into equally likely outcomes. Five design principles are stated: two objects with two names; the event before its probability; modal judgements (certain, possible, impossible) on sets before numbers; the algebra of events taught as such, with the rules derived from it; the sample space as a modelling choice, with frequencies last, as statistical estimates, and the separation repeated for conditional probability and random variables. They are confronted with the probability chapters, from age 9 to 18, of the French-curriculum courses published at https://commeunjeu.org, with research and other curricula. In primary school events precede probabilities without set notation, which comes at age 12; the lessons apply the principles and prove the rules from events in lower secondary school. But, in the version analysed, events account for 18 to 44 percent of the exercises, proofs are hidden in upper secondary school, and automatically corrected calculations record only the number. It proposes number-free tasks on events for ages 6 to 8 and changes to the International Baccalaureate curriculum. No empirical evaluation is reported; hypotheses are stated.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33975v1</id>
    <title>A Pythagoras Tree Grown from a Dodecahedron</title>
    <updated>2026-10-25T01:15:55Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33975v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.33975v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The Pythagoras tree of A. E. Bosman (1942) is drawn with squares in the plane and, in the three-dimensional versions we know of, with cubes. This article documents a tree built instead from regular dodecahedra: each dodecahedron carries five smaller copies, one on each edge of a single pentagonal "crown" face, scaled by $g \approx 0.4346$ and twisted by $45^\circ$ about the edge. The construction first existed only as a pair of rendered images and two undocumented C++ programs. We recover its exact parameters from the original Blender scene, reformulate it as an iterated function system with condensation, and prove with a short computer-assisted argument that it never collides with itself: two of its dodecahedra overlap only when one is the parent of the other. A Pythagorean identity for the six face axes of the dodecahedron singles out the scale $1/\sqrt{5}$ and the twist $\arccos(1/\sqrt{5})$. With these values each child rests flat against a face of its parent, the five children together have exactly the parent's surface area, and the crown of the tree is a fractal of Hausdorff dimension exactly 2. Finally we ask whether the tree can grow on all twelve faces at once. A parity argument shows that at the artwork's proportions it cannot, but smaller scale factors admit certified clash-free all-faces trees.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32273v1</id>
    <title>On the Algebraic Structure of Lewis Carroll's Logic -- Behind the Looking Glass: A Mathematical Perspective</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T07:32:30Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32273v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32273v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Charles Ludwidge Dodgeson, better known by his literary pen name `Lewis Carroll', has a number of well known and cherished literary works to his credit, for example "Alice in Wonderland" and "Through the Looking Glass". Apart from this he is known to have a strong professional interest in mathematics and logic with an inclination towards an educational and recreational perspective.
  In this work we consider the algebraic structure behind Lewis Carroll's approach to classical logic and his logical puzzles. Starting with the arithmetic of $0$ and $1$, we develop the connections between Boolean-valued functions, sets and predicates, which we refer to as the "entangled trinity". This provides a common setting in which Carroll's approach and Boole's perspective can be understood. Particular attention is given to what is meant by "the conclusion" of a logical problem. We suggest a precise interpretation of a complete conclusion in terms of largest lower bounds involving only the predicates to be retained, thereby sharpening Carroll's approach. The role of natural language in choosing a suitable universe and identifying these predicates is discussed through a variety of examples. Finally, we present computerised solution methods, including the use of Boolean satisfiability solvers for larger puzzles.</summary>
    <category term="math.HO" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31804v1</id>
    <title>Research profiles and the mathematical landscape: A grassroots proposal for mathematics with AI</title>
    <updated>2026-10-22T18:41:59Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31804v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.31804v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Repeated mathematical work with AI leaves behind corrections, failed arguments, and sometimes useful ways of asking questions. I propose keeping these in a research profile that the mathematician develops and controls. The profile marks parts of the mathematical landscape according to the researcher's understanding and makes those markings available to later work with AI. This suggests experiments with individual profiles, shared readings of papers, and graduate education. It also raises mathematical questions about the landscape itself: its connections, distances, and changes under discovery. I describe two examples, searching for branches of mathematics with a common base and recovering useful questions from the history of Floer theory. The aim is to give mathematicians something to try and a part in deciding how mathematical AI develops.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33104v1</id>
    <title>Formalising John Dee's Monas Hieroglyphica in Lean 4</title>
    <updated>2026-10-22T16:07:44Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33104v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.33104v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>John Dee's Monas Hieroglyphica (Antwerp, 1564) contains twenty-four numbered theorems about a single composite alchemical glyph, presented in the manner of Euclid: theorem, demonstration, corollary. In this note the following question is considered: which of Dee's theorems can be stated precisely in a proof assistant, and which of them can then be proved? Working in Lean 4 (v4.35.0) with the core library only (without Mathlib), we divide the treatise into three layers: the syntax of the glyph, encoded as inductive data; Dee's arithmetic, verified by kernel computation; and the geometry of the final theorems, in connection with which we prove a classical result not stated by Dee: no ratio of whole numbers doubles the cube, that is, the cube root of two is irrational (the Delian obstruction). The accompanying file Monas.lean compiles with no errors and no sorry. Two observations are made. The cabalistic computation of Theorem XVII, according to which the Cross, "by the best kabbalistic computation," signifies the number 252, is verified, and its proof depends on no axioms: it is a pure computation. The only theorem of the formalisation with genuine mathematical content, the Delian obstruction, is proved constructively and depends only on the axioms propext and Quot.sound.</summary>
    <category term="math.HO" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>
